summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
tangentialFactors:
The assessment gap between LGBTQ+ travellers as a whole and trans travellers in Manila, 69 against 62, indicates that risk in the Philippines attaches more to visible gender non-conformity than to sexual orientation as such. The same assessment rates HIV-positive travellers higher at 81, which suggests the acute exposure for trans visitors lies in presentation and documentation rather than in health-status screening.

The absence of a national anti-discrimination statute leaves protection dependent on where a visitor is. Eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities have SOGIE ordinances, so the practical coverage of the Safe Spaces Act and local ordinances varies sharply between the capital and provincial areas. Local bans on cross-dressing, in Marawi since 2004 and Kabacan since 2019, are the clearest example of how far that patchwork can run in the restrictive direction.

Academic and human-rights reporting connects the legal vacuum to harm. A 2017 international human-rights report, 'Just Let Us Be', documented bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools at a time when the law offered few remedies. Reporting notes a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts among LGBTQ Filipinos, and documents hate crimes and forced conversion therapy carried out by family members against LGBTQ teenagers in a major religious denomination, backed by that church's central establishment.

The institutional response to detainees illustrates two divergent practices. Manila City Jail leaves protection to inmate hierarchies and forced informal pairings, while BJMP-Davao segregates LGBT detainees into a separate annex as it does for other vulnerable groups. Neither model provides gender-matched placement or recognition of legal gender.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing protections are sectoral rather than general. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers carries a 20,000 to 40,000 peso fine and/or up to one year for SOGIE harassment, while the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act provide for fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days and a sensitivity seminar for slurs and ridicule. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Educational measures are in place. The Department of Education and the DSWD allowed students in late 2016 to wear uniforms matching their gender identity, the July 2017 Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy reviews curricula for gender stereotypes and designates June as Pride Month, and the rules of the 2013 Anti-Bullying Law list sexual orientation and gender identity among prohibited bullying grounds.

Legal gender recognition for residents remains judicial only, with the 2008 Supreme Court ruling barring change even after gender-affirming surgery. The proposed recognition bill would open X and non-binary markers, including for minors with consent, and its drafter Chase Go states that the absence of a recognition process drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence.

Community organisations that formed from the 2000s onwards concentrate on sexual health, particularly HIV, psychosocial support and spiritual needs, alongside counselling and therapy services used to help people leave dangerous and hostile environments. Since gender-diverse people experience a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts, these services carry weight beyond their numbers.

Registered LGBTQ couples in Quezon City can exercise medical and health decisions for each other through the Right to Care Card introduced in June 2023, first in government-owned hospitals. The armed forces have accepted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender on the birth certificate.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa rules are not covered by the available sources. Whether a trans visitor's passport gender marker, entry stamp or screening process creates an outing risk at Philippine ports of entry remains unresolved and unsourced here, as does any requirement to present documents matching presentation.

The legal weight of the local cross-dressing ordinances could not be verified beyond their reported terms. Marawi City's December 2004 ordinance and Kabacan's November 2019 prohibition are reported as carrying imprisonment, but enforcement frequency, current validity and any court challenge are not sourced in this inventory.

The status of the SOGIE Equality Bill and of the trans legal gender recognition bill is unresolved as to enactment. Sources describe both as pending, the equality bill stalled for some 25 years and the recognition bill intended for endorsement to the 20th Congress on 28 July, but no source confirms passage or the current session's outcome.

The relationship between Republic Act 11166, which the inventory describes as prohibiting discrimination tied to sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and the absent national SOGI anti-discrimination law is not reconciled in the sources. Whether RA 11166 supplies a general remedy or is limited in scope to HIV-related discrimination is unresolved here.
